Triggers.value: Feeling physically restrained or held down

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the simultaneously severe, poorly processed trauma-memory profile implied by 'Full Sensory Reliving' and 'Olfactory Recall'. Those latter items suggest intrusive sensory re-experiencing, while very easy verbal access points in the opposite direction and is hard to reconcile in the same profile without additional context.

The Threat node is not coherent internally: 'Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating' is a non-threat/cognitive impairment item, whereas the other threat items are specific hypervigilant danger-monitoring states ('Waking Alert', 'Startle to Movement'). This makes the Threat selections thematically inconsistent.

Cross-node coherence is weak around 'Triggers: Being Followed'. That trigger implies a persecutory/social-tracking danger theme, but the rest of the profile centers more on restraint, safety checking, startle, and sensory reliving, without corresponding appraisals or memories about pursuit/tracking. It feels insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation.

'Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Going Out' is not well linked to the selected trigger/threat pattern. The profile emphasizes tiredness, restraint sensations, night-time safety checking, and movement-related startle, but not a clear outside/public-space threat theme. Avoiding going out therefore appears mismatched to the rest of the selected content.

vignette: Lena, a 19-year-old European-American dancer, has been struggling significantly since the man-made disaster that occurred several months ago. The traumatic event was a building collapse at a dance studio during an annual performance. Lena had come to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it. This sense of injustice has made her feel as though she no longer belongs anywhere, contributing significantly to the difficulties she faces in her daily life. Lena's memories of the event are vividly sensory; when the memory comes back, it feels completely real across all her senses at once. She can still smell the acrid scent of smoke and hear the shattering glass, which often brings her back to that terrifying moment. These full-sensory relivings of the experience have led Lena to avoid going out and engaging in activities she used to enjoy. The fear of being followed or feeling restrained is especially acute when she is outside, leading her to cover her face with her hands and retreat into isolation. The overwhelming sense of not belonging has exacerbated Lena's aversion to public spaces. She had come to believe that if she thinks about the event, she will not be able to handle it, so she actively avoids any situation that might trigger those memories. This avoidance behavior has led her to give up on many activities that once brought her joy and fulfillment as a dancer. Lena's concentration has been severely impacted by her trauma. She often wakes during the night to check whether she is safe and feels startled by unexpected movements nearby, perceiving them as threats. These heightened states of alertness have contributed to her feeling very tired or exhausted throughout the day. The fatigue further amplifies her sense of being followed or restrained, creating a cycle that tightens over time. Lena's maladaptive strategies have reinforced these triggers and negative appraisals. By avoiding going out and giving up pleasant activities, she has inadvertently created a self-reinforcing loop where her fear and exhaustion worsen. This avoidance also isolates her from social support and distracts her from the routines that would help alleviate some of her symptoms. The consequences of Lena's behavior have been significant in her daily life as a dancer. She no longer performs or attends rehearsals, which has led to strain with her colleagues and coaches who do not fully understand what she is going through. Her concentration issues have also made it difficult for her to focus on choreography and dance techniques, leading her to withdraw from performances. What frightened Lena most was the realization that her life had changed irrevocably since the disaster. The combination of feeling deeply unfair about the situation and knowing that she cannot find words to describe what happened has led her to believe that she no longer belongs anywhere. This sense of disconnection from others and herself is a significant source of distress. Finally, Lena sought help because she realized that she could not continue living in constant fear and isolation. She hopes for a way to reclaim her life as a dancer without being haunted by the traumatic memories that have taken over her daily existence.
